status: complete — 219 of 222 verses; 7:26-28 is unindexed by decision (see coverage_note); awaiting second-pass review
note: Twelve chapters of a wise man testing everything under the sun and reporting what he found. One entry carries a prior citation, 3:11 from the Scriptural Appendix, which assigns the book to C06 and C24. The indexing order expected PR04 and C18; both are reached repeatedly, and that density is the book's character, not an index stretched to fill.
genre_note: The book argues with itself. Observations made 'under the sun' are set beside counsels that answer them, and the Preacher's own despair is recorded without correction. The index uses the mode field to keep these apart: an observation of what fails — wealth hoarded, labour without end, a king who can no longer be told anything — is a counter-example; a counsel the book commends is prescribes; the Preacher's own search and its limits are exemplifies. Nothing the Preacher says in despair is tagged as though the book commended it. The refrain to eat, drink, and enjoy one's work recurs six times and is tagged with its practice once, at its fullest statement (9:7-10), so that the count reflects one anchor rather than six.
prediction_note: Three practices previously unanchored anywhere in the index were tested here. PR28 is tagged for the first time, at 2:1-11, as a counter-example of medium confidence: the passage shows surplus spent on aesthetic expansion and its emptiness, though not the redirection to the poor that completes the practice. PR24 and PR27 are not reached. The drafter expected none of this; the indexing order placed PR28's strongest candidates in Acts and 2 Corinthians, which remain the better tests of the practice's positive form.
coverage_note: 7:26-28 — the woman whose heart is snares, and 'one man among a thousand have I found; but I have not found a woman among all those' — is left out. Read plainly it is a bitter generalisation the book does not itself build on, and its one conclusion is stated in the next verse, 7:29, which is indexed. Indexing 7:26-28 would require either endorsing the generalisation or explaining it away, and both were declined, as with the oracles against the nations in Jeremiah. The remaining verses are indexed, many at medium confidence: the book is aphoristic in chapters 7 and 10, and short pericopes were preferred there to clusters because the sayings follow a discernible thread.

entries.pericope: Vanity of vanities; there is no new thing under the sun
entries.connection: The thesis is stated before any argument: everything is breath, vapour, and the world's motions — sun, wind, rivers — return on themselves without arriving. 'The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.' C18's detachment begins from exactly this observation, that nothing under the sun can bear the full weight of a human want.

entries.pericope: In much wisdom is much grief
entries.connection: Wisdom applied to everything finds its own limit: what is crooked cannot be made straight, what is lacking cannot be counted, and increase of knowledge is increase of sorrow. C02 treats wisdom as a skill; the Preacher shows the skill pressed past what it can do. The limit is reached in grief rather than accepted as a discipline, which is why the Discipline of Unknowing is tagged later in the book, where it is, and not here, where the limit is only suffered.

entries.pericope: I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards
entries.connection: A man in surplus does with it exactly what the Heavenly Palace warns against: houses, vineyards, gardens and parks, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers — 'whatever my eyes desired, I didn't keep from them.' Then he looks at all of it: 'behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.' PR28 asks a household in surplus to resist the pull toward luxurious upgrades and aesthetic expansion and to treat the relief of the afflicted as the true architecture. This is the fullest scriptural account of the first half of that practice's absence and what it costs the one who builds. The redirection to the poor, the second half, is not in the passage, which is why the entry is a counter-example rather than a prescription and why confidence is medium. The first anchor for PR28 anywhere in the index.

entries.pericope: So I hated life
entries.connection: Wise and fool die alike and are alike forgotten; what a man builds he must leave to someone who may be a fool. The Preacher's conclusion is stated without softening — 'I hated life,' 'I began to cause my heart to despair' — and 'even in the night his heart takes no rest.' The restless heart is C22's subject and the impossibility of keeping what one labours for is C18's. PR08 was considered: the despair is honestly voiced and preserved in scripture uncorrected. But it is spoken to himself rather than brought before God, which is the practice's definition, and Sacred Lament's anchors in Psalms and Job are the better ones.

entries.pericope: Nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good
entries.connection: The first appearance of the book's refrain, which recurs at 3:12-13, 3:22, 5:18-20, 8:15, and 9:7-10: the good available under the sun is to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in one's work, and this too 'is from the hand of God.' The ordinary received as gift is C28's liturgy and C10's gratitude. The refrain is tagged with its practice at its fullest statement, 9:7-10.

entries.pericope: For everything there is a season
entries.connection: Fourteen pairs of opposites, each with its time. Wisdom as knowing what the time is — C02's skill of living — rather than knowing what is right in the abstract. And the sequence of planting and plucking, weeping and laughing, is the shape C25 gives to growth: it has seasons, and none of them can be skipped or hurried.

entries.pericope: He has also set eternity in their hearts
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix names 3:11 as the anchor of the Discipline of Unknowing: God has set eternity in human hearts, 'yet so that man can't find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.' A longing for the whole, and an inability to grasp it, given together and by the same hand. The response the Preacher draws is not scepticism but to rejoice, to do good, and to fear — which is the practice's own guard against confusing unknowing with indecision.

entries.pericope: In the place of justice, that wickedness was there
entries.connection: Wickedness found where justice should be, and two responses held side by side: 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked,' and the bleak comparison of human and animal death. C01's claim that conduct is not a matter of indifference to God is asserted here against the evidence rather than read off it. The question 'who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward' is left as the Preacher's question; the index does not answer it for him.

entries.pericope: The tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter
entries.connection: Oppression seen from below: tears, power on the side of the oppressors, and 'they had no comforter,' said twice. C16's argument for why the vulnerable specifically matters is this observation turned into a responsibility. PR21 was considered. The comfortless are exactly whom Verbal Almsgiving seeks out, but the passage describes the condition the practice exists to address, not the practice or its absence, and the review brief's rule on Micah 7:1-6 applies.

entries.pericope: Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor
entries.connection: Work driven by rivalry — 'the envy of a man's neighbor' — and a man alone, with no son or brother, whose labour has no end and who never asks, until too late, 'for whom then, do I labor?' Against both, a handful with quietness. C18's freedom from accumulation and C22's quiet soul, with envy named as the engine of the restlessness.

entries.pericope: If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow
entries.connection: Two are better than one because when one falls the other lifts him, and 'woe to him who is alone when he falls.' The plainest argument in the wisdom books for a shared life: not ideal, just stronger, warmer, harder to break. C13's ordinary faithfulness and C14's household.

entries.pericope: An old and foolish king who doesn't know how to receive admonition any more
entries.connection: Age and office are no protection against folly once a man can no longer be told anything: the poor wise youth is better than the king who has stopped receiving correction. C02 makes teachability the entrance to wisdom, and C16 observes that authority corrupts nearly everyone who holds it; the king shows both at once.

entries.pericope: To draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools
entries.connection: Approach to God governed by listening, and by few words — 'for God is in heaven, and you on earth.' Then vows: pay what you vow, and better not to vow than to vow and not pay. C09's entrance into the secret place, and C13's vow, which is the Ruth vow kept. PR30's guard against assuming God is persuaded by volume of speech is close in subject, but PR30 is defined as the Lord's Prayer at three fixed hours, and this is not that.

entries.pericope: Wealth kept by its owner to his harm
entries.connection: The oppression of the poor sits inside a hierarchy in which every official is watched by a higher one, which is C16's world of power. Then the lover of silver who is never satisfied, the rich man who cannot sleep, and 'wealth kept by its owner to his harm' — lost in a bad venture, leaving nothing for his son, and in any case left at death: 'naked shall he go again as he came.' Habitual Almsgiving names hoarding from fear as one of the two failures it guards against; this is that failure, and its cost, described.

entries.pericope: God occupies him with the joy of his heart
entries.connection: The refrain again, with something added: the power to enjoy what one has is itself a separate gift, and the one who has it 'shall not often reflect on the days of his life; because God occupies him with the joy of his heart.' C10's joy as a consequence of where one stands, not something manufactured, and C28's day received rather than mastered.

entries.pericope: Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire
entries.connection: Riches without the power to enjoy them; a hundred children and long life with a soul 'not filled with good'; labour for the mouth while 'the appetite is not filled.' The counsel at 6:9 — better what the eyes have than the wandering of desire — is C18's freedom stated as a preference, and the restless desire it warns against is one of C20's four arrivals at the gate.

entries.pericope: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting
entries.connection: The house of mourning is better because 'that is the end of all men, and the living should take this to heart.' C28's witness is Psalm 90:12, teach us to number our days, and this is the same counsel given as a direction for where to spend an evening. 'By the sadness of the face the heart is made good': sorrow that softens rather than curdles, which is the test C19's practice of lament sets. PR08 itself is not tagged, since no grief is being brought before God here.

entries.pericope: The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit
entries.connection: Patience over pride, and anger that 'rests in the bosom of fools' — C22's measure of a healed heart is exactly how quickly anger arrives and how long it stays. The paragraph ends in unknowing: prosperity and adversity set side by side 'to the end that man should not find out anything after him.' The counsel 'don't say, Why were the former days better than these?' belongs to the same humility: a refusal to measure the present against a remembered past one did not actually live in.

entries.pericope: Your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others
entries.connection: In a situation of friction — overhearing one's own servant curse you — the counsel is not to take every word to heart, and the reason given is a look at one's own portion: 'often your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others.' That is Self-Accusation in its exact form, a discipline of sequence in which one's own part is examined before the other's is assigned, and it sits in the chapter, C22, where the curriculum teaches it. 'Surely there is not a righteous man on earth, who does good and doesn't sin' supplies the ground, and C04's audit.

entries.pericope: I said, 'I will be wise;' but it was far from me
entries.connection: The wisest man in the book reports that wisdom was far from him: 'That which is, is far off and exceedingly deep. Who can find it out?' And he keeps seeking. Unknowing as the practice defines it — not abandoning the search, not claiming its end — enacted by the person with the most standing to claim mastery.

entries.pericope: God made man upright; but they search for many schemes
entries.connection: The one conclusion the Preacher says he reached in his search: humans were made upright, and the trouble is what they have gone looking for. C01's grain of reality and C21's diagnostic principle in a sentence — failure traced not to the making but to the seeking. The verses immediately before (7:26-28), on the snaring woman and the one man in a thousand, are left unindexed; see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: His wise heart will know the time and procedure
entries.connection: Counsel for living under a king: keep his command 'because of the oath to God,' do not persist in what is evil, and know that 'there is a time and procedure for every purpose.' Civil obedience with its limit and its ground placed above the throne is C17's. Discerning the time is C02's wisdom. The paragraph ends on what no one has power over — the spirit, the day of death — and on 'a time in which one man has power over another to his hurt.'

entries.pericope: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily
entries.connection: A diagnosis: when judgment is delayed, 'the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.' The interior consequence of an exterior delay, traced as C21 traces a failure to its root. Then the Preacher affirms that it will be better with those who fear God and, in the next breath, that the righteous sometimes receive what the wicked deserve. C01's moral order held as a conviction against counter-evidence the book refuses to hide.

entries.pericope: Even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won't be able to find it
entries.connection: The clearest statement in the book of the limit, and of the danger of denying it: 'however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he won't find it. Yes even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won't be able to find it.' The righteous and their works are 'in the hand of God,' and what lies ahead is not known. The Discipline of Unknowing's formula — unknowing protects the mind from arrogance — and its warning against the man who is humble in character but intellectually insufferable, aimed at the wise specifically.

entries.pericope: To him who is joined with all the living there is hope
entries.connection: One event comes to all, the good and the sinner alike, and the dead are forgotten. And yet: 'to him who is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.' Hope located in being alive rather than in being admirable, which is C19's door at its plainest. The impermanence of love, hatred, and envy alike is C18's.

entries.pericope: Go your way — eat your bread with joy
entries.connection: The refrain at its fullest and most imperative: eat your bread with joy, drink your wine with a merry heart, live joyfully with the wife you love, and whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might — 'for God has already accepted your works.' The Sacrament of the Ordinary locates the highest expression of the road in the least glamorous settings, and there is no other location available; this is that claim, made by a book that has tried every glamorous setting first and found them empty. The household is C14's and the day is C28's.

entries.pericope: Time and chance happen to them all
entries.connection: The race is not to the swift, nor bread to the wise; 'man also doesn't know his time.' The limits of human control stated as observation rather than complaint, which is the ground C24 asks the reader to stand on. It shares PR04's subject; the posture is tagged at the entries where the Preacher prescribes or enacts it.

entries.pericope: Yet no man remembered that same poor man
entries.connection: A poor wise man saves a besieged city, and no one remembers him. The Preacher concludes that wisdom is better than strength 'nevertheless the poor man's wisdom is despised.' C23's unrecognised good, though here the hiddenness is imposed rather than chosen, which is why PR13 is not tagged. 'The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools' is C22's quiet soul as a principle of speech.

entries.pericope: Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to send forth an evil odor
entries.connection: 'So does a little folly outweigh wisdom and honor.' The disproportion between a small thing and what it ruins is the governing logic of Watchfulness — the same logic the index tags at James 3:3-6 — and the reason the practice attends to what arrives at the gate before it is large enough to seem worth attention.

entries.pericope: Gentleness lays great offenses to rest
entries.connection: When a superior's anger rises against you, 'don't leave your place; for gentleness lays great offenses to rest.' The counsel is to add nothing to the fire — neither flight nor answer — and to let gentleness do its work. That is Absorbing the Blow in its prudential form; the practice adds the interior half, holding the angry person with pity, which the proverb does not supply, so confidence is medium. The inverted order that follows — folly in high places, princes walking like servants — is C16's world of corrupted authority.

entries.pericope: If the axe is blunt… skill brings success
entries.connection: Every activity carries its own risk — the pit-digger, the wall-breaker, the stone-cutter — and the blunt axe needs more strength where sharpening would have needed less. C02's opening claim, that wisdom is a skill rather than an intelligence, is this image: competence in the doing, learned, and worth more than force.

entries.pericope: A fool also multiplies words
entries.connection: Gracious words from the wise; from the fool, speech that begins in foolishness and ends in 'mischievous madness,' multiplied because he does not know what will be. The speech audit of C04, which asks first where one was dishonest, unkind, or exaggerating, finds its counter-portrait here.

entries.pericope: Don't curse the king, no, not in your thoughts
entries.connection: Two kinds of neglect: a land whose rulers feast in the morning, and a house whose roof sinks 'by slothfulness.' C13's ordinary faithfulness is the opposite of both. The closing counsel reaches inward — not even in your thoughts, not even in your bedroom — which is C20's attention to what is entertained before it is spoken.

entries.pericope: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don't withhold your hand
entries.connection: Give a portion to seven, even to eight, 'for you don't know what evil will be on the earth' — generosity spread widely and repeatedly, which is Habitual Almsgiving's rhythm (medium: some read 11:1-2 as commercial counsel). Then the core of the passage: as you don't know the way of the wind or how bones grow in the womb, 'you don't know the work of God'; therefore sow in the morning and in the evening. The Discipline of Unknowing says explicitly that it is not indecision — one can act steadfastly while knowing one's understanding is partial. Here the not-knowing is given as the reason to act, not to wait. 'He who observes the wind won't sow' is the failure the practice guards against.

entries.pericope: Rejoice, young man, in your youth… but know
entries.connection: Joy is commanded — the light is sweet, rejoice in all your years — and accountability is set beside it without cancelling it: 'but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.' C10's joy and C01's moral seriousness held in one instruction to the young.

entries.pericope: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth
entries.connection: The allegory of ageing — the keepers of the house trembling, the grinders few, the windows darkened, desire failing — ends with the silver cord severed and the spirit returning to God. Remember before the evil days come. C28's numbering of days, and C18's detachment from a body and a life that will be given back.

entries.pericope: Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man
entries.connection: The epilogue, in another voice, sums the book: fear God and keep his commandments, 'for God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.' C01's ground, and the premise beneath C23: the hidden good is not lost, because nothing hidden is unseen. The warning about the endlessness of making books is left to speak for itself.
